hook_stories.text: Sarah is shopping online for a new backpack. She finds two deals: Deal A: Buy 2 backpacks for $40; Deal B: Buy 3 backpacks for $60. She wants to know which deal offers the better price per backpack. Which deal has the lower price per backpack?
hook_stories.closing_line: Proportional reasoning helps us understand how things relate to each other. Whether we're comparing prices or seeing how much someone recycled, this skill helps us make smart decisions!

hook_stories.text: The Canadian government is planning a recycling program. In one neighborhood, 50 people recycled 200 kg of materials in one week. In another neighborhood, 30 people recycled 120 kg in a week. Which neighborhood had a higher average amount of items recycled per person?
hook_stories.closing_line: Proportional reasoning helps us understand how things relate to each other. Whether we're comparing prices or seeing how much someone recycled, this skill helps us make smart decisions!

explanation_steps: Proportional relationships are when two quantities change together at a constant rate.
We can figure out how much one quantity is for one unit of another — this is called the unit rate or constant of proportionality.
If a recipe needs 2 cups of flour for every 1 cup of sugar, the ratio is 2:1.
For every 1 kg of apples, the price is $3.00. This is a unit rate of $3/kg.

To tell if a relationship is proportional: all ratios are the same, graphs form a straight line through the origin (0,0), and equations are in the form y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality.
concept.whiteboard_text: Proportional relationships: constant rate, unit rate, y = kx
concept.comprehension_check:
Which table shows a proportional relationship?
| A | B |
|---|- |
| x | y |
| 1 | 5 |
| 2 | 10 |
| 3 | 15 |

| C | D |
|---|- |
| x | y |
| 1 | 5 |
| 2 | 10 |
| 3 | 12 |

A) Table A  B) Table B  C) Both A and B  D) Neither A nor B
reteach_angles: Think of proportional relationships as consistent ratios - when one quantity doubles, the other doubles too.
A helpful way to test proportionality is to divide each y value by its corresponding x value; if all the results are the same, then it's proportional.

problems.text: A family plans to travel 300 km. They drive at a constant speed and cover 60 km in 1 hour. How far will they go in 4 hours?
problems.answer_explanation: They travel at 60 km/h. In 4 hours, they will go 60 km/h × 4 h = 240 km.
problems.common_misconception: Confusing multiplying by 4 with adding 4 hours or adding 60 km four times instead of multiplying by 4.

intervention_hints.level_1: Think: How far does the family go in 1 hour?
intervention_hints.level_3: They go 60 km in 1 hour, so in 4 hours, they go 60 × 4 = 240 km.

problems.text: A recipe for cookies says: 'Use 4 eggs for every 2 cups of flour.' How many eggs are needed for 6 cups of flour?
problems.answer_explanation: For 1 cup of flour, we need 4 ÷ 2 = 2 eggs. So for 6 cups, we need 2 × 6 = 12 eggs.
problems.common_misconception: Mixing up the relationship, such as thinking 4 eggs for 6 cups means 4 × 6 = 24 eggs instead of finding the unit amount first.

intervention_hints.level_1: Try making a ratio table of eggs to flour
intervention_hints.level_2: How many eggs for 1 cup of flour? Then multiply by 6 cups
intervention_hints.level_3: If 4 eggs = 2 cups, then 1 cup = 2 eggs, so 6 cups = 6 × 2 = 12 eggs.

problems.common_misconception: Thinking 25% of 80 = 25 × 80 = 2000 instead of converting to a fraction or decimal.

intervention_hints.level_2: Turn 25% into a fraction or decimal (25/100 = 1/4)

problems.text: The price of a bicycle went from $200 to $240. What was the percent increase?
problems.answer_explanation: The increase is $40. To find percent, divide 40 by 200 and multiply by 100. So 40 ÷ 200 = 0.2 = 20%.
problems.common_misconception: Calculating percent increase using the new price or not dividing correctly by the original amount.

intervention_hints.level_2: Then divide the difference by the original price and multiply by 100
intervention_hints.level_3: Increase is $40. Divide 40 by original $200 to get 0.2 or 20%

problems.text: A basketball player scored 20 baskets in 5 games. If he continues scoring at the same rate, how many baskets will he score in 12 games?
problems.answer_explanation: In one game, he scores 20 baskets ÷ 5 games = 4 baskets per game. So for 12 games, he’ll score 4 × 12 = 48 baskets.
mc_choices: 4 baskets per game; 48 baskets in 12 games
4 baskets per game; 60 baskets in 12 games
5 baskets per game; 60 baskets in 12 games
5 baskets per game; 48 baskets in 12 games
problems.common_misconception: Assuming that he keeps scoring at the same rate but confusing the final step of calculation.

intervention_hints.level_1: First, work out how many baskets he scores in one game
intervention_hints.level_2: Then you can use that to find how many he scores in 12 games
intervention_hints.level_3: He scored 20 baskets in 5 games, so 20 ÷ 5 = 4 baskets per game. Then 4 × 12 = 48 baskets

problems.nova_guiding_question: First, work out how many baskets he scores in one game. Then you can use that to find how many he scores in 12 games.

problems.text: A restaurant orders 200 kg of rice to last 5 weeks. At this same rate, how much rice will they need for 12 weeks?
problems.answer_explanation: They use 200 kg ÷ 5 weeks = 40 kg per week. So for 12 weeks, they’ll need 40 × 12 = 480 kg.
problems.common_misconception: Mixing up the calculation or doubling the original amount when the weeks are more than double.

intervention_hints.level_1: Find how much rice is used per week

problems.text: A car travels at 60 km/h. How far will it travel in 3.5 hours?
problems.answer_explanation: Distance = Speed × Time. So 60 km/h × 3.5 h = 210 km.
problems.common_misconception: Adding time or not correctly calculating 3.5 × 60.
